slides.narration: A kite flies in the wind, a boat crosses a river, a ball is hit across a field. None of these can be described by one number on one line. We need quantities with direction. In this part we meet vectors, learn to add, subtract and resolve them, and then study two ways of multiplying them.

slides.heading: Scalars and vectors
slides.body_md: Some quantities need only a size; others also need a direction.
bullets: **Scalar**: magnitude and unit only (mass, time, distance, speed, energy). Scalars add like ordinary numbers.
**Vector**: magnitude, unit **and** direction, and it obeys the vector addition law (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force).
A vector is drawn as an arrow: length = magnitude, arrowhead = direction. In print it is written $\vec{A}$ and its magnitude as $|\vec{A}|$ or $A$.
Two vectors are **equal** if they have the same magnitude and direction, wherever they are drawn.

rows: Mass, time, speed, distance, temperature, energy
Magnitude and a sense, but do not obey the vector addition law

visual.alt: Table comparing scalars and vectors with examples and how each is added

slides.narration: A scalar is fixed by a number and a unit, like a mass of five kilograms. A vector also needs a direction, like a velocity of five metres per second towards the north. Vectors are drawn as arrows. Two arrows with the same length and direction represent equal vectors, wherever on the page they are drawn.

slides.heading: Multiplying a vector by a real number
slides.body_md: For a real number $\lambda$, the vector $\lambda\vec{A}$ has magnitude $|\lambda|A$.
bullets: If $\lambda > 0$ it points the same way as $\vec{A}$; if $\lambda < 0$ it points the opposite way.
$-\vec{A}$ has the same magnitude as $\vec{A}$ and the opposite direction; $\vec{A} + (-\vec{A}) = \vec{0}$, the **null vector**.
The **unit vector** along $\vec{A}$ is $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/A$: magnitude one, no unit, only direction.

slides.narration: Multiply a vector by two and it becomes twice as long, with the same direction. Multiply by one half and it is half as long. Multiply by minus one and you get an arrow of the same length pointing the opposite way. A vector divided by its own length is a unit vector: it carries only the direction.

slides.heading: Adding vectors: triangle and parallelogram laws
slides.body_md: Displacements show how vectors add: walk along $\vec{A}$, then along $\vec{B}$.
bullets: **Triangle law**: place the tail of $\vec{B}$ at the head of $\vec{A}$; the resultant $\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$ joins the tail of $\vec{A}$ to the head of $\vec{B}$.
**Parallelogram law**: draw $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ from one point; the diagonal from that point is $\vec{R}$.
Vector addition is **commutative** ($\vec{A}+\vec{B}=\vec{B}+\vec{A}$) and **associative**.
Magnitudes do not simply add: $R \le A + B$, with equality only for parallel vectors.

slides.narration: Draw the two vectors from one point and complete the parallelogram. The diagonal from that point is the resultant. If you instead place the second vector at the head of the first, you reach the same point: that is the triangle law. The order does not matter, but the lengths do not simply add up.

slides.heading: Magnitude and direction of the resultant
slides.body_md: For $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ with angle $\theta$ between them (tail to tail):
bullets: $\alpha$ is the angle of $\vec{R}$ from $\vec{A}$.
Largest resultant $A + B$ at $\theta = 0^\circ$; smallest $|A - B|$ at $\theta = 180^\circ$; at $\theta = 90^\circ$, $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$.
So the magnitude of the resultant of two vectors lies between $|A-B|$ and $A+B$.

slides.narration: By the law of cosines on the triangle, the resultant has size given by the square root of A squared plus B squared plus two A B cosine theta. Its angle from A comes from the tangent formula. The resultant is largest when the vectors are parallel, smallest when they are opposite, and always lies between those limits.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two cables on a signboard post
slides.body_md: Two cables pull a signboard post in a Pune market with forces of $6$ kN and $4$ kN, at $60^\circ$ to each other. Find the magnitude of the resultant pull and its direction relative to the 6 kN cable.
bullets: $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{4\sin 60^\circ}{6 + 4\cos 60^\circ} = \dfrac{3.46}{8} = 0.433$, so $\alpha = 23.4^\circ$.
The resultant is $8.72$ kN, $23.4^\circ$ from the 6 kN cable towards the 4 kN cable.

slides.narration: Put six and four into the formula with sixty degrees between them. Six squared is thirty six, four squared is sixteen, and two times six times four times cosine of sixty is twenty four. The sum is seventy six, so the resultant is 8.72 kilonewtons. The tangent formula then gives an angle of 23.4 degrees from the six kilonewton cable.

slides.heading: Subtracting vectors
slides.body_md: $\vec{A} - \vec{B}$ is defined as $\vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$.
bullets: Reverse $\vec{B}$ and add; or join the head of $\vec{B}$ to the head of $\vec{A}$ (both tails together) and the arrow runs from $\vec{B}$ to $\vec{A}$.
Subtraction is **not** commutative: $\vec{B} - \vec{A} = -(\vec{A} - \vec{B})$.
For the vectors of Example 1: $|\vec{A}-\vec{B}| = \sqrt{36 + 16 - 24} = 5.29$.

slides.heading: Resolving a vector; unit vectors
slides.body_md: Any vector in a plane is the sum of two perpendicular components.
bullets: $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ are unit vectors along $+x$ and $+y$.
$\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j}$ with $A_x = A\cos\theta$ and $A_y = A\sin\theta$.
Conversely $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$ and $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$; take care of the quadrant.
A resolved component is independent of the other: this idea makes projectile motion easy.

slides.heading: Adding by components (the analytical method)
slides.body_md: Add the x parts and the y parts separately.
bullets: If $\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$ then $R_x = A_x + B_x$ and $R_y = A_y + B_y$.
This works for any number of vectors, and subtraction and scaling work the same way.
Finish with $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$ and $\tan\theta = R_y/R_x$.

rows: λ A_x î + λ A_y ĵ

slides.narration: The analytical method is the most reliable. Resolve every vector along x and y, add the x components, add the y components, and then rebuild the resultant from its two components. It works for any number of vectors and for subtraction and scaling too.

slides.heading: Scalar (dot) product
slides.body_md: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$, a **scalar**.
bullets: Geometric meaning: $A$ times the component of $\vec{B}$ along $\vec{A}$ (or the other way round).
Commutative and distributive: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A}$.
$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A} = A^2$; $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k} = 1$ and $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = 0$ etc.
In components: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$. Zero for perpendicular vectors.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: angle between a force and a displacement
slides.body_md: A force $\vec{F} = (6\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})$ N acts on a trolley that is displaced by $\vec{d} = (3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j})$ m. Find $\vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}$ and the angle between them.

slides.heading: Vector (cross) product
slides.body_md: $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = AB\sin\theta\ \hat{n}$, a **vector**.
bullets: Direction: perpendicular to both, by the **right-hand rule** (curl the fingers from $\vec{A}$ to $\vec{B}$; the thumb gives $\hat{n}$).
Magnitude $AB\sin\theta$ = area of the parallelogram on $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Zero for parallel vectors.
**Not commutative**: $\vec{B}\times\vec{A} = -\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$.
$\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = (A_yB_z - A_zB_y)\hat{i} + (A_zB_x - A_xB_z)\hat{j} + (A_xB_y - A_yB_x)\hat{k}$.

slides.heading: Cross products of the unit vectors
slides.body_md: In the cyclic order $\hat{i} \to \hat{j} \to \hat{k} \to \hat{i}$ the product is positive; in the reverse order it is negative.
bullets: $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j}\times\hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{i} = \hat{j}$.
$\hat{i}\times\hat{i} = \hat{j}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}\times\hat{k} = \vec{0}$.
These nine results generate the component formula.

visual.alt: Table of the cross products of the unit vectors i, j and k: cyclic order gives plus, reverse order gives minus

slides.narration: Remember the cycle: i, j, k, and back to i. A product taken along the cycle gives plus the third vector; taken against the cycle it gives minus. A unit vector crossed with itself is zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a cross product in the plane
slides.body_md: Let $\vec{A} = (2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j})$ and $\vec{B} = (4\hat{i} - 1\hat{j})$. Find $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$, the angle between the vectors and the area of the triangle they span.
bullets: $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = (A_xB_y - A_yB_x)\hat{k} = (2)(-1) - (3)(4) = -2 - 12 = -14$, so $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = -14\,\hat{k}$ (into the page).
$AB\sin\theta = 14$ with $A = \sqrt{13}$ and $B = \sqrt{17}$: $\sin\theta = 0.942$ and $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 5 > 0$, so $\theta = 70.3^\circ$ (acute).
Triangle area $= \tfrac{1}{2}|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}| = 7$ square units.

slides.heading: Dot and cross products compared
slides.body_md: Two products, two different jobs.
bullets: Use the **dot** product to find an angle, a projection, or a scalar such as work.
Use the **cross** product to find an area, a perpendicular direction, or a vector such as torque (later chapters).

rows: A times the projection of B on A

visual.alt: Table comparing the scalar product and the vector product

slides.narration: The dot product gives a scalar and is zero for perpendicular vectors. The cross product gives a vector and is zero for parallel vectors. One is commutative, the other changes sign when the order is swapped.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Magnitude + direction; obeys triangle / parallelogram law
R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ); |A − B| ≤ R ≤ A + B
A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ; A = A_x î + A_y ĵ
A B cos θ = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z (scalar)
A B sin θ, right-hand rule (vector); area of parallelogram

visual.alt: Summary table of vector addition, subtraction, components and the two products

slides.narration: To sum up. Vectors add by the triangle or parallelogram law, or by adding components. Subtraction is addition of the reversed vector. Any vector in a plane is the sum of its components along the axes. The dot product gives a scalar and the cross product a vector.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: State the angle between the vectors clearly: tail to tail for the resultant formula.
Resolve and add components when there are three or more vectors, or when the angle is awkward.
Check the quadrant of an angle from the signs of the components before using the tangent.
Dot product: scalar, A B cos θ. Cross product: vector, A B sin θ, and say its direction.

rows: A times the projection of B on A

visual.alt: Table comparing the scalar product and the vector product

slides.narration: Always say which angle you are using. With three or more vectors, resolve and add components. Check the quadrant from the signs of the components. And for products, remember the dot gives a number and the cross gives a vector whose direction you must state.

slides.heading: Position, velocity and acceleration in a plane
slides.body_md: In a plane each is a vector with two components.
bullets: Position vector $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j}$; displacement $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1$.
Velocity $\vec{v} = d\vec{r}/dt = v_x\hat{i} + v_y\hat{j}$ is always **tangent to the path**; acceleration $\vec{a} = d\vec{v}/dt$.

For **constant acceleration**: $\vec{v} = \vec{u} + \vec{a}t$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{r}_0 + \vec{u}t + \tfrac{1}{2}\vec{a}t^2$, which split into two independent one-dimensional sets (chapter 2), one for $x$ and one for $y$.

rows: u sin θ · t − ½ g t²

visual.alt: Table of the horizontal and vertical components of acceleration, velocity and position of a projectile

slides.narration: In a plane, position, velocity and acceleration are all vectors with an x part and a y part. The velocity is always tangent to the path. When the acceleration is constant, the equations of straight line motion apply separately along x and along y, and the two parts combine as vectors.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: constant acceleration in a plane
slides.body_md: A particle starts from the origin with velocity $3\hat{i}$ m s$^{-1}$ and has a constant acceleration $(1\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})$ m s$^{-2}$. Find its position, velocity, speed and the direction of its velocity at $t = 4$ s.
bullets: Speed $= \sqrt{49 + 64} = 10.6$ m s$^{-1}$; direction $\tan\theta = 8/7$, $\theta = 48.8^\circ$ above $+x$.

functions.label: path of the particle: x = 3t + 0.5t², y = t²

visual.alt: Path in the x y plane of a particle that starts along the x-axis and accelerates in x and y: a curve bending upward that reaches x equal 20 metres and y equal 16 metres at 4 seconds
visual.caption: The path is a curve, although each component moves with constant acceleration.

slides.narration: Treat x and y separately. In four seconds x grows to 20 metres and y to 16 metres. The velocity components are 7 and 8 metres per second, so the speed is 10.6 metres per second at 48.8 degrees above the x axis. The path curves upward.

slides.heading: Projectile motion: two independent motions
slides.body_md: A **projectile** moves under gravity alone (air resistance neglected). Its acceleration is $g$ downward everywhere.
bullets: **Horizontal:** no acceleration, so $v_x$ is constant.
**Vertical:** acceleration $-g$, as for a body thrown up or dropped.
The two motions are **independent**: time is the common link.
Evidence: a ball dropped and a ball thrown horizontally from the same height reach the ground together.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: horizontal projection from a cliff
slides.body_md: A stone is thrown horizontally at $20$ m s$^{-1}$ from the top of a cliff $78.4$ m high ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$). Find the time of flight, the horizontal range, and the speed and direction of the stone as it lands.
bullets: Vertical: $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gT^2$, so $T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(78.4)}{9.8}} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ s.
Range $R = uT = 20 \times 4 = 80$ m.
At landing $v_x = 20$ and $v_y = gT = 9.8 \times 4 = 39.2$ m s$^{-1}$ downward; $v = \sqrt{400 + 39.2^2} = 44.0$ m s$^{-1}$, at $\tan^{-1}(39.2/20) = 63.0^\circ$ below the horizontal.

visual.alt: Path of a ball thrown horizontally at 20 metres per second from a height of 78.4 metres: half of a downward-opening parabola that reaches the ground 80 metres away
visual.caption: Horizontal projection: half a parabola.

slides.narration: The fall takes the same time as a drop from the cliff: 4 seconds. In that time the stone moves 80 metres sideways. Just before landing its vertical speed is 39.2 metres per second and its horizontal speed is still 20, so it hits at 44.0 metres per second, 63.0 degrees below the horizontal.

slides.heading: Projectile at an angle: the equation of path
slides.body_md: Launch speed $u$ at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal: $u_x = u\cos\theta$, $u_y = u\sin\theta$.
bullets: Eliminating $t$ gives $y = ax - bx^2$: a **parabola**.
Velocity at time $t$: $v_x = u\cos\theta$, $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$; the speed is least at the top.

slides.heading: Time of flight, maximum height and range
slides.body_md: For a launch and landing at the same level:
bullets: $T$: set $y = 0$. $H$: set $v_y = 0$ (at time $T/2$). $R = u\cos\theta\times T$.
$R$ is greatest at $\theta = 45^\circ$, where $R_{max} = u^2/g$; then $H = R_{max}/4$.
Angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$ give the **same range**.
$\dfrac{H}{R} = \dfrac{\tan\theta}{4}$.

visual.alt: Range against angle of projection for a speed of 20 metres per second: a symmetric hump about 45 degrees with a maximum of 40.8 metres
visual.caption: The range curve is symmetric about 45°.

slides.narration: Setting the height to zero gives the time of flight. Setting the vertical velocity to zero gives the maximum height. Multiplying the horizontal speed by the time of flight gives the range, u squared sine two theta over g. The range is greatest at forty five degrees, and two angles that add to ninety degrees give the same range.

slides.heading: Same speed, different angles
slides.body_md: A ball thrown at 20 m s$^{-1}$ at five angles:
bullets: The 15° and 75° paths have the same range; the 30° and 60° paths too.
Larger angle: higher and longer in the air; but beyond 45° the range falls again.

visual.alt: Five trajectories of a ball thrown at 20 metres per second at 15, 30, 45, 60 and 75 degrees: the 45 degree path has the longest range, 40.8 metres, and the 15 and 75 degree paths have the same range, 20.4 metres
visual.caption: Same speed 20 m s⁻¹; complementary angles give equal ranges.

slides.narration: All five balls leave at twenty metres per second. The forty five degree path goes farthest. The paths at fifteen and seventy five degrees land at the same place, but the steeper one climbs much higher and stays in the air longer.

slides.heading: What changes along the path
slides.body_md: Velocity and acceleration while a projectile rises, tops out and falls:
bullets: The **acceleration** is $g$ downward throughout, including at the top.
At the top $v_y = 0$ but $v_x = u\cos\theta \neq 0$, so the speed there is $u\cos\theta$, the minimum.
It lands with the launch speed (same level) at the angle $\theta$ below the horizontal.

rows: up and forward, vertical part shrinking
down and forward, vertical part growing

visual.alt: Table of velocity and acceleration of a projectile while rising, at the top and while falling

slides.narration: The acceleration never changes: gravity pulls down all the time. At the top only the vertical velocity vanishes, so the speed there is u cosine theta, the smallest on the path. On landing at the launch level the speed is the launch speed again.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: the longest throw
slides.body_md: A fielder can throw a cricket ball a greatest horizontal distance of $90$ m on level ground. Find her throwing speed, and the maximum height and time of flight when she throws at $45^\circ$.
bullets: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin 45^\circ}{g} = \dfrac{2 \times 29.7 \times 0.7071}{9.8} = 4.29$ s.

visual.alt: Range against angle of projection for a speed of 20 metres per second: a symmetric hump about 45 degrees with a maximum of 40.8 metres
visual.caption: The range curve is symmetric about 45°.

slides.narration: The greatest range occurs at forty five degrees and equals u squared over g. So the speed is 29.7 metres per second. At that angle the height is a quarter of the range, 22.5 metres, and the flight takes 4.29 seconds.

slides.heading: Uniform circular motion: angular speed
slides.body_md: A body moving on a circle at constant speed.
bullets: **Period** $T$: time for one revolution; **frequency** $f = 1/T$.
**Angular speed** $\omega = \Delta\theta/\Delta t = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f$ (rad s$^{-1}$); $\theta$ must be in radians.
Speed $v = \omega r = 2\pi r/T$; the speed is constant, the **velocity is not** (its direction changes).
Every point on a rotating disc has the same $\omega$ but a speed proportional to its radius.

visual.alt: Table of period, frequency, angular speed, speed and centripetal acceleration for uniform circular motion

slides.narration: Angular speed is the angle swept per second, measured in radians. It equals two pi over the period. The speed along the circle is omega times the radius. Although the speed is constant, the velocity keeps changing direction.

slides.heading: Centripetal acceleration
slides.body_md: Compare the velocities at two points separated by angle $\Delta\theta$.
bullets: As $\Delta\theta \to 0$, $\Delta\vec{v}$ points **to the centre**: the acceleration is **centripetal**.
Two arrows of equal length $v$ and an angle $\Delta\theta$ between them form an isosceles triangle.

slides.heading: Velocity along the tangent, acceleration to the centre
slides.body_md: $a = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$, directed toward the centre, perpendicular to $\vec{v}$.
bullets: At fixed $r$: $a \propto v^2$. At fixed $v$: $a \propto 1/r$. At fixed $\omega$: $a \propto r$.
Because $\vec{a} \perp \vec{v}$ the acceleration changes only the direction of the velocity, not the speed.

sections.heading: 1. Scalars and vectors; addition, subtraction and resolution
sections.body_md:
- A **scalar** has magnitude and unit only; a **vector** also has direction and obeys the vector addition law. Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force are vectors; mass, time, distance, speed and energy are scalars.
- Multiplying $\vec{A}$ by a real number $\lambda$ gives a vector of magnitude $|\lambda|A$, along $\vec{A}$ if $\lambda>0$ and opposite if $\lambda<0$. The **unit vector** is $\hat{A}=\vec{A}/A$.
- **Triangle law** (head to tail) and **parallelogram law** (tail to tail): $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}$ and $\tan\alpha = B\sin\theta/(A+B\cos\theta)$. Always $|A-B|\le R\le A+B$. For 6 and 4 units at 60° the resultant is 8.72 units at 23.4° from the first.
- **Subtraction:** $\vec{A}-\vec{B}=\vec{A}+(-\vec{B})$; $|\vec{A}-\vec{B}|=\sqrt{A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta}$ (5.29 for the same vectors). It is not commutative.
- **Resolution:** $A_x=A\cos\theta$, $A_y=A\sin\theta$, $\vec{A}=A_x\hat{i}+A_y\hat{j}$. To add vectors by components: add the $x$ parts and the $y$ parts, then $R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}$ and $\tan\theta=R_y/R_x$ (check the quadrant). Three forces of 12, 10, 8 N at 0°, 120° and 240° give 3.46 N at 30.0°.

sections.heading: 2. Scalar and vector products
sections.body_md:
- **Scalar (dot) product:** $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=AB\cos\theta=A_xB_x+A_yB_y+A_zB_z$, a scalar; it equals $A$ times the projection of $\vec{B}$ on $\vec{A}$; commutative; zero for perpendicular vectors; $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A}=A^2$.
- **Vector (cross) product:** $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=AB\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, with $\hat{n}$ perpendicular to both by the right-hand rule; its magnitude is the area of the parallelogram on $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$; zero for parallel vectors; $\vec{B}\times\vec{A}=-\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$.
- Unit vectors: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}=0$, $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=1$; $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}$, $\hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}$ and the reverse orders give a minus sign.
- Example: $(6\hat{i}+2\hat{j})\cdot(3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}) = 10$, angle 71.6°. For $\vec{A}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B}=4\hat{i}-\hat{j}$, $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=-14\hat{k}$, so the triangle on them has area 7.

sections.heading: 3. Motion in a plane and projectile motion
sections.body_md:
- In a plane $\vec{r}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}$, $\vec{v}=d\vec{r}/dt$ (tangent to the path) and $\vec{a}=d\vec{v}/dt$. For constant $\vec{a}$ the $x$ and $y$ motions are independent: $\vec{r}=\vec{r}_0+\vec{u}t+\tfrac{1}{2}\vec{a}t^2$. Example: $\vec{u}=3\hat{i}$, $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}$ gives $\vec{r}=(20\hat{i}+16\hat{j})$ m and speed 10.6 m s⁻¹ at $t=4$ s.
- **Projectile** (only gravity, $a=-g$ downward): $x=u\cos\theta\,t$, $y=u\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, path $y=x\tan\theta-gx^2/(2u^2\cos^2\theta)$, a parabola. Horizontal velocity is constant; at the top $v_y=0$ and the speed is $u\cos\theta$.
- Level ground: $T=2u\sin\theta/g$, $H=u^2\sin^2\theta/2g$, $R=u^2\sin2\theta/g$; $R_{max}=u^2/g$ at $45^\circ$, $\theta$ and $90^\circ-\theta$ give equal ranges, $H=R\tan\theta/4$. For $u=39.2$ m s⁻¹ at 30°: $T=4$ s, $H=19.6$ m, $R=135.8$ m ($g=9.8$ m s⁻²).
- **Horizontal projection** from height $h$ at speed $u$: $T=\sqrt{2h/g}$, range $uT$; from 78.4 m at 20 m s⁻¹: 4 s and 80 m, landing at 44.0 m s⁻¹.
- If landing is not at the launch level, solve $y=0$ (or $y=-h$) as a quadratic in $t$ instead of using the level-ground formulas.

sections.heading: 4. Uniform circular motion
sections.body_md:
- Motion on a circle at constant speed: period $T$, frequency $f=1/T$, **angular speed** $\omega=2\pi/T=2\pi f$ (rad s⁻¹, angles in radians), $v=\omega r$. The velocity is tangent to the circle and changes direction, so the body accelerates although its speed is constant.
- **Centripetal acceleration:** $a=v^2/r=\omega^2 r$, directed towards the centre, perpendicular to $\vec{v}$. Derivation: $|\Delta\vec{v}|=2v\sin(\Delta\theta/2)\approx v\Delta\theta$ and $\Delta t=r\Delta\theta/v$.
- At fixed $r$, $a\propto v^2$; at fixed $v$, $a\propto 1/r$; at fixed $\omega$, $a\propto r$.
- Example: a bike at 54 km h⁻¹ on a 60 m radius track: $v=15$ m s⁻¹, $\omega=0.25$ rad s⁻¹, $a=3.75$ m s⁻². A point on the equator has $a=0.0338$ m s⁻² with $R=6.4\times10^6$ m.
- The average velocity over one full turn is zero (zero displacement); the average speed is $2\pi r/T$.

key_terms.definition_md: Angle swept per unit time, ω = 2π/T, in rad s⁻¹.
The acceleration v²/r = ω²r of uniform circular motion, directed to the centre.

questions.stem_md: A weather bulletin for Chennai lists: temperature 31 °C, wind speed 18 km/h, wind blowing from the north-east at 18 km/h, rainfall 12 mm. Which entry is a vector?

options.text_md: wind blowing from the north-east at 18 km/h

questions.solution_md: A vector needs a direction as well as a magnitude. Only the wind with its direction (from the north-east) qualifies; the speed alone, the temperature and the rainfall depth are scalars — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The mass of a gas cylinder is given by a number and a unit only, with no direction; such a quantity is called a ___ quantity.
questions.solution_md: A quantity with magnitude and unit but no direction is a **scalar**.

questions.stem_md: True or false? For any two vectors A and B, the vector A − B is the same as the vector B − A.
questions.solution_md: False. B − A = −(A − B): the two have equal magnitudes but opposite directions, so subtraction of vectors is not commutative.

questions.stem_md: Two forces of 7 N and 3 N act together at a point. Which of the following cannot be the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.solution_md: The resultant lies between |7 − 3| = 4 N (opposite directions) and 7 + 3 = 10 N (same direction). 4 N, 6 N and 10 N lie in this range; 12 N does not — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Three coplanar forces can keep a body at rest (zero resultant) only if they can form the sides of a closed triangle. Which set of magnitudes can do this?
questions.solution_md: The largest force must not exceed the sum of the other two. 8 ≤ 4 + 5 = 9 holds for 4 N, 5 N, 8 N; 8 > 5, 10 > 8 and 3 > 2 fail for the other sets — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two tugboats pull a barge in a Kochi harbour with forces of 5.0 kN and 8.0 kN. The angle between the two ropes is 60°. Find the magnitude of the resultant force, in kN (3 significant figures).

marking_scheme.step: Law of cosines: R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ

questions.stem_md: For the two tugboat forces of 8.0 kN and 5.0 kN with 60° between the ropes, find the angle the resultant makes with the 8.0 kN rope, in degrees (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta} = \dfrac{5.0\sin 60^\circ}{8.0 + 5.0\cos 60^\circ} = \dfrac{4.33}{10.5} = 0.412$, so $\alpha = 22.4$ degrees.

marking_scheme.step: tan α = B sin θ / (A + B cos θ) with A = 8.0, B = 5.0

questions.stem_md: A porter pulls a luggage trolley along a level platform with a rope that makes 30° with the ground and carries a tension of 80 N. The component of the pull along the ground is
questions.solution_md: The component along the ground is F cos θ = 80 cos 30° = 69.3 N. Using sin gives the vertical component 40.0 N, and 80 tan 30° is not a component of anything here — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The components of a velocity are 9.0 m/s along +x and 12.0 m/s along −y. The velocity points
questions.solution_md: tan θ = 12/9, so θ = 53.1° measured from +x; the y-component is negative, so it lies below the axis — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The unit vector along the vector 3î − 4ĵ is
questions.solution_md: The magnitude is √(9 + 16) = 5, and the unit vector is the vector divided by its magnitude: (3î − 4ĵ)/5 = 0.6î − 0.8ĵ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two vectors are A = 5î + 2ĵ and B = 2î − 6ĵ (SI units). Find the magnitude of A − B (3 significant figures).

**Assertion (A):** Two vectors of equal magnitude P, with an angle of 120° between them, have a resultant of magnitude P.

**Reason (R):** The magnitude of the resultant is √(P² + P² + 2P² cos θ), and cos 120° = −½.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R = √(P² + P² + 2P² (−½)) = √(P²) = P. Both statements are true and R is exactly the working that gives A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A hockey ball moving east at 24 m/s is deflected by a stick so that it moves north at 7.0 m/s. Find the magnitude of the change in its velocity, in m/s.
questions.solution_md: The change in velocity is $\Delta\vec{v} = \vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1 = \vec{v}_2 + (-\vec{v}_1)$: 7 m/s north together with 24 m/s west, two perpendicular parts. $|\Delta\vec{v}| = \sqrt{24^2 + 7^2} = 25.0$ m/s.

marking_scheme.step: Δv = v₂ − v₁ = v₂ + (−v₁): 7.0 m/s north and 24 m/s west

questions.stem_md: A surveyor’s displacement A is 20 m east and displacement B is 15 m north. The vector A − B has magnitude and direction
questions.solution_md: A − B = A + (−B) = (20, 0) + (0, −15) = (20, −15). Its magnitude is 25 m and it points 36.9° south of east — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a scalar and a vector quantity, giving two examples of each from the motion of a cricket ball.

answer.model_answer_md: A **scalar** has magnitude and unit only (the distance it travels, its speed, its mass). A **vector** also has a direction and adds by the triangle law (its displacement from the bat, its velocity, the force of the bat on it). Speed is the magnitude of velocity; velocity needs a direction as well.

questions.solution_md: Magnitude only vs magnitude and direction; two examples each.

marking_scheme.step: Scalar: magnitude only; vector: magnitude and direction (triangle law)

questions.stem_md: What is meant by resolving a vector into rectangular components? Write the components of a vector of magnitude A inclined at an angle θ to the x-axis.

answer.model_answer_md: Resolving a vector means writing it as the sum of two perpendicular vectors along chosen axes. For a vector of magnitude A at angle θ to the x-axis the components are **A_x = A cos θ** along x and **A_y = A sin θ** along y, so A = A_x î + A_y ĵ.

questions.solution_md: Sum of perpendicular parts; A cos θ and A sin θ.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning: sum of two perpendicular vectors along the axes
A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ

questions.stem_md: A vector A is multiplied by the real number −3. State the magnitude and direction of the result, and say what the unit vector along A is.

answer.model_answer_md: The result −3A has magnitude **three times** that of A and points in the direction **opposite** to A, because the number is negative. The unit vector along A is **Â = A/A**: it has magnitude one, no unit, and the direction of A.

questions.solution_md: 3A long, reversed; unit vector A/|A|.

marking_scheme.step: Unit vector = A divided by its magnitude

questions.stem_md: State the parallelogram law of vector addition. Using it, write the expression for the magnitude of the resultant of two vectors A and B inclined at an angle θ, and state when the resultant is largest and when it is smallest.

answer.model_answer_md: If two vectors are drawn from a point as adjacent sides of a parallelogram, the diagonal from that point gives their resultant. Its magnitude is **R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)**. R is largest, A + B, when θ = 0° (the vectors are parallel), and smallest, |A − B|, when θ = 180° (opposite).

questions.solution_md: Law; R formula; limits.

marking_scheme.step: Statement: diagonal of the parallelogram is the resultant
Largest A + B at 0°, smallest |A − B| at 180°

questions.stem_md: (a) State the triangle law of vector addition and write the formulas for the magnitude and direction of the resultant of two vectors A and B with an angle θ between them. (b) Two perpendicular forces of 24 N and 7 N act at a point. Find the magnitude of their resultant and its angle with the 24 N force. (c) Between what limits can the resultant of these two forces lie, if the angle between them could be changed?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Triangle law:** if two vectors are drawn head to tail, the third side from the tail of the first to the head of the second represents their sum. The resultant has magnitude $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$ and makes an angle $\alpha$ with $\vec{A}$ given by $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}$.

(b) At $\theta = 90^\circ$: $R = \sqrt{24^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25$ N. $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{7}{24} = 0.292$, so $\alpha = 16.3$ degrees from the 24 N force.

(c) The resultant is least, $24 - 7 = 17$ N, when the forces are opposite and greatest, $24 + 7 = 31$ N, when they act in the same direction.

questions.solution_md: Triangle law and formulas; 25 N at 16.3°; limits 17 N to 31 N.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md: A survey drone leaves a warehouse in Indore, flies 120 m due north to a water tank and then turns and flies 90 m due east to a gate, before stopping. Take east as the positive x direction and north as the positive y direction.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) 210 m and 150 m

**(b)** 150 m

**(c)** (i) The displacement has $\tan\phi = \dfrac{90}{120} = 0.750$, where $\phi$ is the angle from north towards east, so $\phi = 36.9^\circ$ **east of north**. It points from the warehouse straight towards the gate, not along either leg.

**OR** (ii) The statement is **wrong**. Displacement is the straight-line vector from the start to the finish: $\sqrt{120^2 + 90^2} = 150$ m, in a direction 36.9° east of north. The 210 m is the **distance**, the length of the route; it is greater because the drone turned.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Distance = 120 + 90 = 210 m (a scalar, the whole route). Displacement = √(120² + 90²) = 150 m (a vector, straight from start to finish) — option (d).

**(b)** $\vec{d} = (90\hat{i} + 120\hat{j})$ m. Magnitude $= \sqrt{90^2 + 120^2} = \sqrt{22500} = 150$ m.

**(c)** (i) tan φ = 90/120; 36.9° east of north.

(ii) Displacement 150 m, distance 210 m.

children.solution_md: Distance = 120 + 90 = 210 m (a scalar, the whole route). Displacement = √(120² + 90²) = 150 m (a vector, straight from start to finish) — option (d).

children.stem_md: Express the drone’s displacement as a vector in terms of î and ĵ and give its magnitude, in m.

answer.model_answer_md: The displacement has $\tan\phi = \dfrac{90}{120} = 0.750$, where $\phi$ is the angle from north towards east, so $\phi = 36.9^\circ$ **east of north**. It points from the warehouse straight towards the gate, not along either leg.

questions.stem_md: For which pair of vectors is the scalar product equal to zero?
questions.solution_md: The dot product is the sum of products of matching components: (2)(3) + (3)(−2) = 0 for the first pair. The other pairs give 13, −13 and 12 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Find the angle between the vectors A = 3î + 4ĵ and B = 5î + 12ĵ, in degrees (3 significant figures).
Find the component of A = 6î + 8ĵ along the direction of B = 3î − 4ĵ.
questions.solution_md: The component of $\vec{A}$ along $\vec{B}$ is $\vec{A}\cdot\hat{B} = \dfrac{\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}}{B} = \dfrac{(6)(3) + (8)(-4)}{\sqrt{9 + 16}} = \dfrac{-14}{5} = -2.80$. The negative sign means A has a component opposite to B.

questions.stem_md: The vectors A = 4î + λĵ + 2k̂ and B = 3î − 2ĵ + 5k̂ are perpendicular. Find the value of λ.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **scalar product** is $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta$, a scalar. The **vector product** is $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = AB\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is perpendicular to both vectors, in the sense given by the right-hand rule (fingers from $\vec{A}$ towards $\vec{B}$, thumb along $\hat{n}$).

(b) $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = (1)(2) + (-2)(2) + (2)(1) = 2 - 4 + 2 = 0$. $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = (-2 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 2)\hat{i} + (2 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 1)\hat{j} + (1 \cdot 2 - (-2)(2))\hat{k} = -6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$. A zero dot product means $\cos\theta = 0$: the angle is $90^\circ$.

(c) The area equals $|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}| = \sqrt{36 + 9 + 36} = 9$ square units (as expected: $AB = 3 \times 3 = 9$ when $\theta = 90^\circ$).

questions.solution_md: Definitions; A·B = 0, A × B = −6î + 3ĵ + 6k̂, 90°; area 9.

questions.solution_md: Fall time: $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gT^2$, so $T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2.5}{9.8}} = 0.505$ s. Horizontal distance $R = uT = 3.0 \times 0.505 = 1.52$ m.

questions.solution_md: The greatest range is $R_{max} = u^2/g = 72$ m. Thrown vertically the height is $H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g} = \dfrac{R_{max}}{2} = \dfrac{72}{2} = 36$ m.

questions.stem_md: A projectile is launched with speed u at an angle θ above the horizontal. Show that its path is a parabola.

Substituting in the second, **y = x tan θ − g x² / (2 u² cos² θ)**. This has the form y = a x − b x², where a and b are constants, which is the equation of a **parabola**.

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive expressions for the time of flight, the maximum height and the horizontal range of a projectile launched from level ground with speed u at an angle θ above the horizontal. (b) A ball is thrown with a speed of 30 m/s at an angle whose sine is 0.8 and cosine is 0.6. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², find its time of flight, maximum height and range.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Resolve the launch velocity: $u_x = u\cos\theta$, $u_y = u\sin\theta$. Vertically $y = u\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. At landing $y = 0$ gives $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$. At the top $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt = 0$, so $t = \dfrac{u\sin\theta}{g}$ and $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$. Horizontally the speed is constant, so $R = u\cos\theta \times T = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$.

(b) $u_x = 30 \times 0.6 = 18$ m/s and $u_y = 30 \times 0.8 = 24$ m/s. $T = \dfrac{2 \times 24}{9.8} = 4.90$ s. $H = \dfrac{576}{19.6} = 29.4$ m. $R = 18 \times 4.90 = 88.2$ m.

Taking g = 9.8 m/s², find the time of flight, the horizontal distance covered, and the speed and direction of the stone as it reaches the water.

(a) Take the launch point as origin with $y$ downward. $x = ut$ and $y = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. Eliminating $t$: $y = \dfrac{g}{2u^2}x^2$, a parabola. The stone reaches depth $h$ when $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gT^2$, so $T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$, and the range is $R = uT = u\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

(b) $T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 44.1}{9.8}} = \sqrt{9} = 3.00$ s. $R = 15 \times 3.00 = 45.0$ m. At the water $v_x = 15$ m/s and $v_y = gT = 29.4$ m/s downward, so $v = \sqrt{225 + 864} = 33.0$ m/s, at $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{29.4}{15} = 63.0$ degrees below the horizontal.

questions.passage_md: To help villagers cut off by floods in Assam, a transport aircraft flies horizontally at 80 m/s at a height of 490 m above a field and releases a food packet. Take g = 9.8 m/s² and neglect air resistance.

**(b)** $T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{980}{9.8}} = \sqrt{100} = 10.0$ s. Horizontal distance $= uT = 80 \times 10.0 = 800$ m.

**(c)** (i) v = √(80² + 98²) = 127 m/s.

questions.stem_md: Two identical cricket balls are thrown with the same speed from the same ground level, one at 20° and the other at 70°. Explain, without calculation, why they land at the same place but one stays in the air longer.

answer.model_answer_md: The angles add up to 90°, so the ranges are equal because R depends on sin 2θ. But the time of flight is 2u sin θ/g: the 70° ball has the larger vertical component of velocity, so it rises higher and stays in the air longer.

questions.solution_md: sin 2θ equal; T ∝ sin θ larger at 70°.

marking_scheme.step: T ∝ sin θ, larger for 70°: greater vertical velocity

questions.stem_md: In a multi-flash photograph of a ball thrown across a field, the images are taken at equal time intervals. The horizontal gaps between successive images are all equal, but the vertical gaps near the launch point are larger than those near the top of the path. This shows that

options.text_md: the horizontal velocity changes while the vertical velocity is constant
the horizontal velocity is constant while the vertical velocity changes
the ball is being pushed forward all along its path

questions.solution_md: Equal horizontal gaps in equal times mean constant horizontal velocity; the vertical gaps shrink on the way up, so the vertical velocity decreases because of gravity — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A graph is drawn of the horizontal range of a ball against its angle of projection (0° to 90°) for a fixed launch speed from level ground, neglecting air resistance. Its shape is

options.text_md: a straight line rising from 0° to 90°
a hump with its maximum at 90°
a hump, symmetric about 45°, with its maximum at 45° and zero range at 0° and 90°
a hump that is not symmetric, with its maximum at 60°

questions.solution_md: R ∝ sin 2θ, which is zero at 0° and 90°, largest at 45°, and equal at θ and 90° − θ, so the graph is symmetric about 45° — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at a steady speed. At any instant the acceleration of the stone is

options.text_md: zero, because the speed does not change
directed towards the centre of the circle, with constant magnitude
directed along the tangent, in the direction of motion
directed away from the centre of the circle

questions.solution_md: The speed is constant, but the velocity changes direction, so there is an acceleration, v²/r, always directed towards the centre — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The hour hand of a wall clock makes one complete turn in 12 hours. Its angular speed is about
questions.solution_md: ω = 2π/T = 2π/(12 × 3600 s) = 1.45 × 10⁻⁴ rad/s. The other options belong to the minute hand (1.74 × 10⁻³), a 24-hour rotation (7.27 × 10⁻⁵) and the second hand (0.105) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two children sit on a merry-go-round turning at a steady rate, one at 1.0 m from the axis and the other at 2.0 m. The ratio of their centripetal accelerations (outer : inner) is
questions.solution_md: Both have the same angular speed ω, and a = ω²r is proportional to r, so the outer child has twice the acceleration — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A scooter goes round a circular track at a steady speed. If its speed is doubled on the same track, its centripetal acceleration becomes
questions.solution_md: a = v²/r with r unchanged: doubling v multiplies a by 2² = 4 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A giant wheel at a fair turns steadily; the time it takes to make one complete revolution is called its ___.
questions.solution_md: The time for one complete revolution is the **period** T (and the frequency is 1/T).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When a body moves in uniform circular motion, its average velocity over one complete revolution is zero although its average speed is not.
questions.solution_md: True. After a full revolution the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero; the path length is 2πr, so the average speed is 2πr/T, not zero.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In uniform circular motion the acceleration of the body points towards the centre of the circle.

**Reason (R):** The speed of a body in uniform circular motion is constant.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but constant speed does not explain the direction of the acceleration. The direction follows from the change of the velocity vector, which points to the centre — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The second hand of a station clock is 0.40 m long. Find the speed of the tip of the hand, in m/s (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The second hand turns once in 60 s: $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi}{60} = 0.105$ rad/s. Speed $v = \omega r = 0.105 \times 0.40 = 0.0419$ m/s.

questions.stem_md: A bus tyre of radius 0.50 m rotates steadily at 300 revolutions per minute. Find the centripetal acceleration of a point on its rim, in m/s² (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi \times 300}{60} = 31.4$ rad/s. $a = \omega^2 r = (31.4)^2 \times 0.50 = 493$ m/s$^2$. (Check: $v = \omega r = 15.7$ m/s and $v^2/r = 493$ m/s$^2$.)

questions.stem_md: A small satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m and takes 5.8 × 10³ s for one revolution. Find its centripetal acceleration, in m/s² (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5.8 \times 10^3} = 1.083 \times 10^{-3}$ rad/s. $a = \omega^2 r = (1.083 \times 10^{-3})^2 \times 7.0 \times 10^6 = 8.21$ m/s$^2$.

questions.stem_md: The Moon goes round the Earth in a nearly circular orbit of radius 3.84 × 10⁸ m in 27.3 days. Find its centripetal acceleration, in m/s² (3 significant figures).
Through what angle, in radians, does the minute hand of a clock turn in 20 minutes? (3 significant figures)
questions.solution_md: The minute hand turns $2\pi$ rad in 60 min. In 20 min: $\theta = 2\pi \times \dfrac{20}{60} = 2.09$ rad (one-third of a turn, 120°).

questions.stem_md: A laboratory centrifuge spins a test tube whose bottom is 0.12 m from the axis at 3000 revolutions per minute. Find the centripetal acceleration at the bottom of the tube as a multiple of g, taking g = 9.8 m/s² (3 significant figures).

Two toy figures stand on a turntable rotating at a steady rate, at distances of 0.20 m and 0.60 m from the axis. Find the ratio of the centripetal acceleration of the outer toy to that of the inner toy.
questions.solution_md: Both turn with the same $\omega$, and $a = \omega^2 r$, so $\dfrac{a_{outer}}{a_{inner}} = \dfrac{r_{outer}}{r_{inner}} = \dfrac{0.60}{0.20} = 3$.

questions.stem_md: A car goes round a circular bend at a constant speed of 54 km/h. Is the car accelerating? Give a reason and state the direction of its acceleration.

answer.model_answer_md: Yes. Acceleration is the rate of change of **velocity**, and the velocity changes direction continually even though the speed is constant. The acceleration, v²/r, is directed **towards the centre of the bend**, at right angles to the velocity.

questions.solution_md: Velocity changes direction; a = v²/r towards the centre.

marking_scheme.step: a = v²/r, towards the centre, perpendicular to v

questions.stem_md: A particle moves with angular speed ω on a circle of radius r. Show that its linear speed is v = ωr.

answer.model_answer_md: In a short time Δt the particle turns through an angle Δθ and covers an arc Δs = r Δθ (angle in radians). The speed is v = Δs/Δt = r (Δθ/Δt) = **ω r**, since ω = Δθ/Δt. In one period it covers 2πr, so also v = 2πr/T.

questions.solution_md: Arc = rΔθ; divide by Δt.

questions.stem_md: Write two expressions for the centripetal acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion. How does it change if (i) the speed is halved at the same radius and (ii) the radius is doubled at the same speed?

answer.model_answer_md: The centripetal acceleration is **a = v²/r = ω²r**, directed to the centre. (i) With r fixed, a ∝ v², so halving the speed makes the acceleration **one quarter**. (ii) With v fixed, a ∝ 1/r, so doubling the radius makes the acceleration **one half**.

questions.solution_md: a = v²/r = ω²r; ¼ and ½.

marking_scheme.step: Halved speed: a becomes one quarter
Doubled radius: a becomes one half

questions.stem_md: Using the change of velocity between two nearby points of a circular path, explain why the acceleration in uniform circular motion points towards the centre and has magnitude v²/r.

answer.model_answer_md: Draw the velocities v₁ and v₂ (equal length v, angle Δθ between them) from one point. Their difference Δv has magnitude **vΔθ** for small Δθ and points **along the radius towards the centre**. The time is Δt = rΔθ/v, so a = Δv/Δt = vΔθ ÷ (rΔθ/v) = **v²/r**, towards the centre.

questions.solution_md: Δv ≈ vΔθ towards the centre; divide by Δt = rΔθ/v.

marking_scheme.step: Δv = vΔθ, directed to the centre as Δθ → 0

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive the expression for the centripetal acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion, using the change of velocity between two close points. (b) Show that it can also be written as ω²r. (c) A motorbike goes round a circular track of radius 15 m at a steady 6.0 m/s. Find its angular speed, its period and its centripetal acceleration.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Let the body move from P₁ to P₂ in a short time $\Delta t$, turning through a small angle $\Delta\theta$. The velocities $\vec{v}_1$ and $\vec{v}_2$ have equal magnitude $v$; drawn from a common point they enclose the angle $\Delta\theta$, so $|\Delta\vec{v}| \approx v\Delta\theta$, directed towards the centre. The arc is $v\Delta t = r\Delta\theta$, so $\Delta t = \dfrac{r\Delta\theta}{v}$. Then $a = \dfrac{|\Delta\vec{v}|}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{v\Delta\theta}{r\Delta\theta/v} = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$.

(b) With $v = \omega r$: $a = \dfrac{\omega^2r^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$.

(c) $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r} = \dfrac{6}{15} = 0.4$ rad/s; $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 15.7$ s; $a = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \dfrac{36}{15} = 2.40$ m/s$^2$.

questions.solution_md: a = v²/r = ω²r; ω = 0.40 rad/s, T = 15.7 s, a = 2.40 m/s².

marking_scheme.step: Δv ≈ vΔθ toward the centre, Δt = rΔθ/v

questions.passage_md: A giant wheel at a fair in Kolkata has riders’ cabins moving on a circle of radius 12 m. The wheel turns steadily and makes one complete revolution in 40 s.

questions.stem_md: Two ants sit on a record spinning on a turntable, one near the rim and the other near the centre. Which quantity is the same for both ants?
questions.solution_md: Both turn through the same angle in the same time, so ω is common; v = ωr and a = ω²r are larger for the ant at the larger radius — option (a).
